lessons.title: Founder Vesting, Reverse Vesting and Leaver Clauses

children.text: Fourteen months into MetroMandi, Vikram takes a job offer he cannot refuse. He walks out holding 3,700 shares, 37% of the company, earned over fourteen months of a journey that will run another eight years without him. Anjali keeps building. Every rupee of value she creates from here makes Vikram richer. Nothing about this is illegal or even unusual. It is simply what happens when founder shares are issued without vesting.

body.text: Vesting turns ownership from a one-day event into a multi-year process. It is not a sign of distrust between co-founders. It is the only thing that makes a big equity promise safe to make.

children.text: Vesting and Reverse Vesting Are Not the Same Thing

markDefs.definition: An arrangement where a founder already holds their shares, but the company or the other founders can buy back the unvested portion at a nominal price if the founder leaves early.

children.text: Employees get options that vest: nothing is theirs until the clock says so. Founders are different, because they already hold shares from the day the company was incorporated. You cannot un-issue them. So founder shares use
, where the shares are held from day one but the company or the remaining founders have the right to buy back whatever has not yet been earned if the founder leaves.

columns.label: Forward vesting (employee options)
points: The employee holds nothing on day one
Options vest over time and must then be exercised and paid for
Unvested options simply lapse when the employee leaves
Governed by the ESOP plan and the grant letter

columns.label: Reverse vesting (founder shares)
points: The founder holds all the shares from day one and votes them
The unvested portion is subject to a buyback or transfer right
If the founder leaves early, unvested shares are bought back at a nominal price
Governed by the founders' agreement, shareholders' agreement and articles of association

children.text: The Standard Schedule: Four Years, One-Year Cliff

The market standard in India, as in most startup ecosystems, is four-year vesting with a one-year cliff. Nothing vests for the first twelve months. At the twelve-month mark, a quarter vests in one go. After that, the rest vests in equal monthly or quarterly instalments over the remaining three years. Here is Vikram's 3,700 shares on that schedule.

body.caption: Vikram's 3,700 founder shares on a four-year schedule with a one-year cliff

body.title: Founder vesting with a one-year cliff (% vested)

children.text: The flat line for eleven months is the cliff doing its job. Someone who leaves in month ten keeps nothing. The vertical jump at month twelve is the reward for staying through the hardest year. After that, vesting is smooth, so nobody is ever more than a month away from earning a little more.

content.caption: Monthly vesting after a one-year cliff

children.text: Vikram left at 14 months. 3,700 × 14 ÷ 48 = 1,079.17, so 1,079 shares vested once rounded down, and 2,621 shares remain subject to buyback. Agreements normally specify that fractional entitlements are rounded down to whole shares, because you cannot allot or transfer a fraction of a share.

At a ₹10 face value buyback price, the 2,621 unvested shares cost ₹26,210 to buy back. If those shares are cancelled, MetroMandi has 7,379 shares left: Anjali 3,900 (52.85%), Sameer 2,400 (32.52%) and Vikram 1,079 (14.62%). If the other founders buy them instead, the total stays at 10,000 and Vikram drops to 10.79%.

stats.label: Anjali's stake after
stats.context: Up from 39% without her buying anything

body.text: Vesting protects the founder who stays, and it also protects the one who leaves. Without it, every departure becomes a fight over the whole stake and often ends in a legal dispute that freezes the cap table. With it, the outcome is arithmetic: months served, shares vested, done. Investors will insist on founder vesting at the first priced round anyway, so agreeing it between yourselves on day one means agreeing it on your own terms.

body.title: Vested shares at 20 months
body.prompt: A co-founder holds 4,800 shares on a four-year schedule with a one-year cliff and monthly vesting thereafter. She resigns after 20 months of service. How many shares have vested, rounded down to a whole share?
body.explanation: She is past the cliff, so vesting is 20 ÷ 48 of the total. 4,800 × 20 ÷ 48 = 2,000 shares vested. The remaining 2,800 shares are subject to buyback at the nominal price set in the agreement.

children.text: Vesting decides how much a departing founder has earned. Leaver clauses decide what happens to what they earned, and the answer depends on how they left. The labels are contractual, not statutory, so the definitions in your agreement are the ones that matter.

body.caption: Typical leaver treatment in an Indian startup shareholders' agreement

cells: Death, permanent disability, or departure agreed by the board
Resignation without cause before the term is up
Usually retained, sometimes a portion is bought back at fair value
Fraud, wilful misconduct, breach of the agreement, competing with the company
Often bought back at the lower of nominal price and fair value

body.text: Read the bad leaver definition word by word before you sign. A clause that treats "failure to meet performance expectations" or "departure for any reason other than death" as bad leaver conduct lets the other side strip shares you actually earned. Bad leaver treatment should be reserved for genuine wrongdoing: fraud, wilful misconduct, a serious breach of the agreement or competing with the company.

children.text: How the Buyback Actually Happens in India

A clause saying "unvested shares shall be bought back" is not self-executing. A company buying back its own shares under Section 68 of the Companies Act, 2013 must satisfy conditions and limits, including a cap on how much can be bought back and a gap between buybacks. That is why most Indian startup agreements do not rely on a company buyback at all. Instead they give the continuing founders, or a person nominated by the company, a call option to buy the unvested shares at a nominal price.

body.title: What happens when a founder leaves

events.title: Fix the leaving date
events.description: The agreement defines the trigger date, usually the last working day or the date of the board resolution accepting the resignation.

events.title: Compute vested and unvested shares
events.description: Apply the schedule to the months actually served, rounding fractional entitlements as the agreement specifies.

events.title: Exercise the call option
events.description: The continuing founders or the company's nominee serve notice to buy the unvested shares at the nominal price set in the agreement.

events.title: Execute the transfer
events.description: A share transfer deed in Form SH-4 is executed with stamp duty paid, the board approves the transfer, and the register of members is updated.

events.title: Update everything else
events.description: Refresh the cap table, record the change in the statutory registers, and reflect it in the next annual return.

body.text: Restrictions on share transfers only bind if they are in the articles of association, not just in a side agreement between founders. A private company's articles restrict the transfer of shares by design, so make sure your vesting, call option and leaver provisions are properly written into them. A founders' agreement alone can leave you with a claim for damages rather than the shares themselves.

body.label: Acceleration on acquisition
body.context: Single trigger accelerates vesting when the company is acquired. Double trigger accelerates only if the acquisition happens and the founder is then terminated or their role is materially changed. Acquirers prefer double trigger, because they are buying the team as much as the business.

body.title: Which departure is which?
body.question: A co-founder resigns after 26 months to join a competitor, in breach of a non-compete in the shareholders' agreement. Under a standard set of leaver clauses, what is the most likely outcome?
options: She keeps all her shares, because 26 months is past the cliff
She loses everything, including the shares that vested in the first 26 months, automatically by law
Her unvested shares are bought back at nominal price, and because joining a competitor is bad leaver conduct, her vested shares can also be bought back at the lower of nominal price and fair value
Nothing happens until the company is sold
body.explanation: Unvested shares always go back on any departure. Bad leaver conduct, which typically includes competing with the company, additionally puts the vested shares at risk on the terms the agreement sets. Nothing happens automatically by law: everything here comes from the contract and the articles of association.

body.title: Name the first year
body.textWithBlank: The initial period during which nothing vests at all, after which a large chunk vests in one go, is called the ___.
body.explanation: A one-year cliff means a founder or employee who leaves in month eleven takes nothing, while someone who completes twelve months immediately earns 25% of a four-year grant.

body.title: The investor wants you to re-vest
body.scenario: You and your co-founder have run a Chennai logistics startup for three years and hold 45% and 35% with no vesting in place. A Series A investor's term sheet requires both founders to put their entire holdings on a fresh four-year vesting schedule starting from closing, with a one-year cliff and single trigger acceleration removed. Your co-founder is furious: "We have already done three years. Why are we starting from zero?"
body.prompt: Is this reasonable, and what would you negotiate?
body.modelAnswer:
Why the investor is asking:
They are funding the next four years of your work, not the last three. If either of you leaves a year after the round, the investor is left paying for a company without the team it backed. Some form of founder vesting at the first priced round is standard and worth accepting in principle.

What to negotiate:
1. Credit for time served. Ask that a meaningful portion of your holdings, often 25% to 50%, be treated as already vested at closing to recognise three years of building. Full re-vesting from zero after three years is aggressive.
2. No cliff on the re-vested portion. You have already proved commitment, so monthly vesting from day one of the new schedule is more appropriate than a fresh twelve-month cliff.
3. Double trigger acceleration. Push back on removing acceleration entirely. Double trigger, where vesting accelerates only if the company is acquired and you are then terminated or materially demoted, protects you without deterring an acquirer.
4. A tight bad leaver definition, limited to fraud, wilful misconduct, serious breach and competing with the company. Never accept performance-based bad leaver language.
5. Symmetry. Whatever applies to one founder should apply to both, and the leaver mechanics should be in the articles of association, not just the shareholders' agreement.

What to tell your co-founder: the vesting protects each of you from the other. It is also far better to negotiate these terms now, while the investor still wants the deal, than to discover them in a dispute later.

body.title: Setting up founder vesting properly
steps: Agree a schedule for every founder, including yourself, and put it in writing before the first outside cheque.
Use four years with a one-year cliff unless you have a specific reason not to.
State the vesting commencement date explicitly, and whether it runs from incorporation or from when each founder went full-time.
Set the buyback or call option price for unvested shares, usually face value or the original issue price.
Define good leaver, early leaver and bad leaver in plain language, and keep bad leaver limited to genuine wrongdoing.
Decide whether acceleration on an acquisition is single or double trigger.
Write the vesting, call option and transfer restrictions into the articles of association, not just the founders' agreement.
Specify how fractional share entitlements are rounded.

cards.definition: Earning ownership over time rather than receiving it all on day one.
Founder shares issued upfront but subject to buyback at a nominal price if the founder leaves before the schedule completes.
An initial period during which nothing vests, followed by a single large vesting event.
A contractual right for the company's nominee or the continuing founders to buy specified shares at an agreed price.
A departing founder whose exit is treated sympathetically, typically keeping all vested shares.
A founder who leaves in circumstances involving wrongdoing, whose vested shares can also be bought back cheaply.
Vesting accelerates only if two events occur: the company is acquired and the founder is terminated or materially demoted.
The share transfer deed used to transfer shares in an Indian company, which must be executed with stamp duty paid.

points: Without vesting, a founder who leaves in year one keeps their entire stake forever.
Founders use reverse vesting: shares are held from day one but the unvested portion can be bought back at a nominal price on an early exit.
The standard is four years with a one-year cliff, then monthly or quarterly vesting.
At 14 months of a 48-month schedule, Vikram earned 1,079 of 3,700 shares. The rest went back for ₹26,210 at face value.
Leaver clauses decide what happens to vested shares, and bad leaver definitions should be limited to genuine wrongdoing.
Company buybacks are restricted under Section 68 of the Companies Act, 2013, so agreements usually use a call option in favour of the continuing founders instead.
Transfer restrictions bind only if they are in the articles of association, so get them written in.
Investors will require founder vesting at the first priced round, so set it yourself first and negotiate credit for time already served.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not legal, tax or investment advice. MetroMandi and the founders described are fictional, and all share counts, schedules and prices are illustrative. Leaver categories and buyback mechanics are contractual and vary from deal to deal, and buyback, transfer and stamp duty requirements change over time and differ by state. Have a qualified company secretary or lawyer draft and review your founders' agreement, shareholders' agreement and articles of association.
